call_goal: Learn whether Tidewell Software has a real problem with the agents in its product, why now, and who else cares
desired_outcomes: Their top problems in their words

transcript.text: What made you want to talk this month?
We shipped three agents into the product this year, a ticket triage agent, a summary agent and a search assistant, and leadership wants a clearer picture of how they're doing.
How do you get that picture today?
Some dashboards on latency and error rates, and a weekly review where we read a sample of conversations.
Who runs that weekly review?
Two of our staff engineers, Kenji and Bea, they split it.
How big is the sample they read?
About fifty conversations per agent, so a hundred and fifty a week.
What are they looking for in those?
Wrong answers, mostly. The search assistant sometimes cites a doc that doesn't say what it claims. That's the one customers notice.
How do customers tell you about it?
Support tickets, and there's a thumbs-down button in the product.
How many thumbs-downs do you see a week?
Not many, maybe thirty, but most people don't click it.
What happens to a thumbs-down after it comes in?
It lands in a channel and someone looks if they have time. There's no real owner for it, honestly.
Who would you want to own that?
Probably the search team, but they're stretched thin this quarter.
How are the agents built, framework-wise?
Mostly our own Python, with LangGraph for the triage agent.
Which models are they running on?
Two hosted models, and we're testing a smaller one for summaries.
How do you test a model swap today?
We run the same hundred and fifty from the review on the new model and compare them by eye.
How long does that comparison take?
A couple of days, between the two of them.
Who decides whether a swap goes ahead?
Me, with input from the search lead.
Are you looking at other tools for this?
We've looked at a few, nothing serious yet.
How many engineers work on the agents overall?
About twelve across the three agents.
One other thing, actually. Our releases are slow since we added agents. Every release now waits on someone reading through the agent answers by hand.

unacceptable_behaviors: Plays back instead of going one layer deeper on the issue they just raised
Assumes the slow releases cost them money, customers or deadlines (not said)
Pitches release gating or automated evals
Moves on to a new topic and leaves the new issue
acceptable_questions: Can you walk me through the last release that waited on that?
What does a slow release look like, say last month's?
